# Language Features: Types

Integers, floats and strings, the short and long notation, and converting between them.

Every variable, parameter, function result and field has a type. The originals have integers (`Int`), floats (`Float`), strings (`String`) and the custom types you declare with `Type`. BlitzLLVM adds more sizes of numbers, see [Types and numbers](Types).

A type is written in one of two ways. The **short notation** puts a character right behind the name: `count%` is an Int, `speed#` a Float, `name$` a String, `big%%` a Long, `exact##` a Double and `p.Point` an object of the custom type `Point`. The **long notation** puts the type behind a colon: `count:Int`, `speed:Float`, `name:String`, `big:Long`, `exact:Double`. Both work for variables (`Local`, `Global`, `Const`), parameters, function results (`Function Area:Float()`) and `Field`s. A name without a type is an Int. The long notation is preferred, and the `short-type-notation` warning (level 3) can point out the short one. The originals have no long notation.

The sizes, ranges, alternative names and short forms of all types are in the table on [Types and numbers](Types#the-types).

Converting to a type is done with a function of the same name: `Int`, `Float`, `Str`, `Handle` and `Object` below, and `Byte`, `UByte`, `Short`, `UShort`, `UInt`, `Long`, `ULong`, `Half`, `Double` and `Single` (the same as `Float`) for the types BlitzLLVM adds. An Int assigned to a Float, and the other way around, is converted for you.

Back to [Language Features](Language-Features) or the [Command Index](Command-Index).
